bibl.title: A Neural Correlate of Working Memory in the Monkey Primary Visual Cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Here, we identify a neural correlate of working memory in the monkey primary visual cortex ( V1).

span.label: visual working memory in primary visual cortex
span.quote: We trained monkeys (Macaca mulatta) to perform a delayed-response task in which the animals had to remember briefly the location of a figure after it had been removed from the visual scene (1).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: During the delayed-response task, multiunit activity of V1 neurons was recorded in two monkeys (2).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Figure-ground contextual modulation in V1, generated by recurrent feedback, is carried on past stimulus offset and thereby converts the sensory representation into a working-memory trace.
span.quote: We therefore propose that contextual modulation in the primary visual cortex is a correlate of the process that forms a bridge between sensory activity and working memory.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Two processes act on V1 during the delay in opposite directions: one suppresses overall firing while a second preserves the figure-versus-ground difference.
span.quote: Thus, whereas one mechanism suppresses overall activity in V1 during the delay, another mechanism seems to be able to maintain the difference in figure versus ground signals.

span.label: The signal recorded in V1 is stated to depend on feedback from higher areas, so the site of the recording is not the site of the process.
span.quote: Contextual modulation in V1 depends on feedback from higher visual areas (7–9), which implies that it is a specific correlate of recurrent processing

span.label: The early figure-ground signal is the same whether the animal later remembers or forgets; only the late persistence separates them.
span.quote: Thus, for correct trials as well as for incorrect trials, the figure is equally well segregated from the ground, as indicated by the presence of contextual modulation in the first 250 ms after stimulus onset

span.label: The memory signal decays with the length of the delay, so its strength depends on how long the animal is asked to wait.
span.quote: This indicates that the strength of contextual modulation is related to the delay period, where modulation becomes weaker for longer delays

span.label: the whole delayed-response experiment repeated with a STATIC orientation-defined figure in place of the moving one, followed by a mask
span.quote: In a control experiment, we observed the same phenomenon when a static, rather than a moving, stimulus was used in the same delayed-response task.

span.label: contextual modulation
span.quote: This late enhancement of the sensory response—contextual modulation—correlates closely with the perception of the figure

span.label: recurrent processing
span.quote: which implies that it is a specific correlate of recurrent processing

span.label: working memory
span.quote: Here, we identify a neural correlate of working memory in the monkey primary visual cortex

span.label: delayed-response task
span.quote: We trained monkeys (Macaca mulatta) to perform a delayed-response task in which the animals had to remember briefly the location of a figure after it had been removed from the visual scene

span.label: receptive fields
span.quote: when the figure dots were overlying the V1 receptive fields

span.label: contextual modulation - AS A CORRELATE OF RECURRENT PROCESSING: a V1 signal whose source is feedback from higher visual areas, so it indexes a loop rather than the area it is recorded in
span.quote: Contextual modulation in V1 depends on feedback from higher visual areas (7–9), which implies that it is a specific correlate of recurrent processing

span.label: the memory signal - DEFINED BY THE ANIMAL'S REPORT: trials are sorted after the fact into correct and incorrect by whether the saccade landed on the remembered location within 500 ms, and the neural difference is computed between those two sets
span.quote: In correct trials, the animal made a saccade toward the figure location within 500 ms after cue time. In incorrect trials, the animal failed to respond correctly within this period

span.label: the figure-ground difference - NOT STIMULUS-DRIVEN BY CONSTRUCTION: the motion on the receptive field was arranged to be identical on average for figure and ground, so the difference cannot be attributed to the local stimulus
span.quote: We arranged the directions of motion such that, on average, the motion stimuli on the RF were identical for the “figure” and “ground” situations

span.label: explains-away → fMRI studies finding little delay activation in early visual areas (ref. 15)
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE MEASURE CAN SEE THE SIGNAL. Two mechanisms run in opposite directions: 'ONE MECHANISM SUPPRESSES OVERALL ACTIVITY IN V1 during the delay, ANOTHER MECHANISM SEEMS TO BE ABLE TO MAINTAIN THE DIFFERENCE IN FIGURE VERSUS GROUND SIGNALS.' A method reading overall activity therefore records a decrease while the memory signal - a DIFFERENCE between two conditions - is maintained. The paper offers this as why 'VERY LITTLE DELAY ACTIVATION IS FOUND IN EARLY VISUAL AREAS' in imaging
span.quote: Thus, whereas one mechanism suppresses overall activity in V1 during the delay, another mechanism seems to be able to maintain the difference in figure versus ground signals. In that sense, the maintained activity is different from delay-period activity recorded in temporal (13) or prefrontal (14) cortex. This difference may also explain why in functional magnetic resonance imaging studies, very little delay activation is found in early visual areas (15).

span.label: distinguishes-from → delay-period activity in temporal (ref. 13) and prefrontal (ref. 14) cortex
span.note: differs in: WHAT IS MAINTAINED DURING THE DELAY. Elsewhere it is the firing rate; here the rate falls and what persists is a CONTRAST between figure and ground - 'In that sense, THE MAINTAINED ACTIVITY IS DIFFERENT FROM DELAY-PERIOD ACTIVITY RECORDED IN TEMPORAL OR PREFRONTAL CORTEX.' Two things called delay activity that a rate measure would score in opposite directions
span.quote: Thus, whereas one mechanism suppresses overall activity in V1 during the delay, another mechanism seems to be able to maintain the difference in figure versus ground signals. In that sense, the maintained activity is different from delay-period activity recorded in temporal (13) or prefrontal (14) cortex. This difference may also explain why in functional magnetic resonance imaging studies, very little delay activation is found in early visual areas (15).

span.label: builds-on → the criterion that stored information is held only if needed (ref. 11)
span.note: differs in: WHETHER PERSISTENCE ALONE DEMONSTRATES STORAGE. The distractor condition supplies the missing half: modulation persists when the figure is the target and decays when the same figure is the distractor, so 'the continuation of modulation is NOT A PASSIVE PROCESS BUT IS RELATED TO AN ACTIVE STORAGE of information needed for the animal's goal'. The same stimulus with the same retinal input yields opposite signals according to task relevance
span.quote: The remaining amount of modulation is much stronger when the figure is relevant to the memory task than when it is not (P , 0.0005). These results indicate that the continuation of modulation is not a passive process but is related to an active storage of information needed for the animal

span.label: recurrent processing —causes→ contextual modulation
span.quote: Contextual modulation in V1 depends on feedback from higher visual areas (7–9), which implies that it is a specific correlate of recurrent processing

span.label: working memory —operationalised-as→ delayed-response task
span.quote: We trained monkeys (Macaca mulatta) to perform a delayed-response task in which the animals had to remember briefly the location of a figure after it had been removed from the visual scene

span.label: p-value
span.quote: During the delay period, the figure response remained stronger than the ground response (Fig. 2B) (P , 1024 for all delay periods).

span.label: regression
span.quote: We then fitted a linear regression line through these data points for each delayedresponse period.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Dotted lines above the (cid:222)gure responses indicate the SEM.

span.label: mean
span.quote: Population average of modulation ratios (see Fig. 3, G and H) for the (cid:222)gure 5 target and (cid:222)gure 5 distractor conditions.

span.label: After the figure was removed from the screen, V1 responses to the figure stayed stronger than responses to the ground throughout the delay, so figure-ground contextual modulation continues in the absence of the stimulus.
span.quote: During the delay period, the figure response remained stronger than the ground response (Fig. 2B) (P , 1024 for all delay periods).

span.label: The strength of the maintained figure-ground modulation shrinks as the required memory delay gets longer.
span.quote: This indicates that the strength of contextual modulation is related to the delay period, where modulation becomes weaker for longer delays.

span.label: Correct and incorrect trials did not differ in the initial figure-ground signal, so the difference between them lies only in whether the signal was maintained.
span.quote: Thus, for correct trials as well as for incorrect trials, the figure is equally well segregated from the ground, as indicated by the presence of contextual modulation in the first 250 ms after stimulus onset.

span.label: In the late part of the delay, contextual modulation vanished entirely on trials where the monkey later made the wrong saccade, while it continued on trials answered correctly.
span.quote: The decrease of modulation was stronger for incorrect trials, and contextual modulation for the incorrect trials disappeared completely in the late part of the delay period (Fig. 3, B and D), whereas modulation for the correct trials continued (Fig. 3, A and C).

span.label: Modulation was maintained only when the remembered figure was the behaviourally relevant target and fell away when the same figure was a distractor, showing that the maintenance is an active, goal-dependent storage rather than a passive after-effect.
span.quote: These results indicate that the continuation of modulation is not a passive process but is related to an active storage of information needed for the animal’s goal.

span.label: During the delay V1 shows two dissociable effects at once: overall firing is suppressed while the figure-versus-ground difference is preserved.
span.quote: Thus, whereas one mechanism suppresses overall activity in V1 during the delay, another mechanism seems to be able to maintain the difference in figure versus ground signals.

span.label: The maintained signal cannot be visual persistence, because it lasts up to about 2 s whereas visual persistence for such stimuli lasts only tens of milliseconds, and it survives replacement of the display.
span.quote: It is highly unlikely that the maintained activity is a neural correlate of visual persistence, i.e., the lasting visibility of a stimulus after its physical disappearance.

span.label: The monkeys detected the figure well overall but their performance dropped as the delay lengthened, confirming the task taxes short-term memory.
span.quote: Detection of the figure was high and declined for longer delay periods (Fig. 2A), indicating that the task requires short-term memory processes.

span.label: The same continued modulation appeared with a static orientation-defined texture figure followed by a mask, so persistence is not an artefact of the motion stimulus.
span.quote: In a control experiment, we observed the same phenomenon when a static, rather than a moving, stimulus was used in the same delayed-response task.

span.label: contextual modulation
span.quote: This late enhancement of the sensory response—contextual modulation—correlates closely with the perception of the figure (4– 6).

span.label: visual persistence
span.quote: It is highly unlikely that the maintained activity is a neural correlate of visual persistence, i.e., the lasting visibility of a stimulus after its physical disappearance.

span.label: relative degree of modulation persistence
span.quote: Dividing the average modulation strength of the last 250 ms before cue time by the modulation strength of the first 250-ms period after stimulus onset gives the relative degree of modulation persistence during the delay period (Fig. 3, G and H).

span.label: correct trial (in the delayed-response task)
span.quote: In correct trials, the animal made a saccade toward the figure location within 500 ms after cue time.

span.label: delay length (latency of the cue time)
span.term: delay length (latency of the cue time)
span.quote: The latency of the cue time was varied between 0 and 2000 ms after stimulus onset.

span.label: task relevance of the figure (second stimulus relevant vs irrelevant)
span.term: task relevance of the figure (second stimulus relevant vs irrelevant)
span.quote: The second stimulus could be either relevant or irrelevant to the delayed-response task.

span.label: strength of contextual modulation
span.quote: We calculated the strength of contextual modulation (3) for the first 250 ms after stimulus onset as an indication of the initial segregation strength of the figure from ground, and for the last 250 ms before cue time as an indication of the signal strength available for responding in the memory task.

span.label: behavioural detection performance across delays
span.quote: Detection of the figure was high and declined for longer delay periods (Fig. 2A), indicating that the task requires short-term memory processes.

span.label: direction of motion falling on the receptive field
span.term: direction of motion falling on the receptive field
span.quote: We arranged the directions of motion such that, on average, the motion stimuli on the RF were identical for the “figure” and “ground” situations (3, 4).

span.label: 28 ms — how long the motion-defined figure was shown before it had to be remembered
span.quote: After a 300-ms fixation, a motiondefined figure appeared very briefly (28 ms) at one of three locations (Fig. 1).

span.label: 0 and 2000 ms — range over which the memory delay (cue-time latency) was varied
span.quote: The latency of the cue time was varied between 0 and 2000 ms after stimulus onset.

span.label: P , 1027 — significance of the decline in modulation strength across the delay for the 1000 and 2000 ms delays
span.quote: For the 1000- and 2000-ms delay periods, there was a significant decline in modulation (P , 1027).

span.label: P , 0.0005 — significance of the difference in remaining modulation between figure-as-target and figure-as-distractor
span.quote: The remaining amount of modulation is much stronger when the figure is relevant to the memory task than when it is not (P , 0.0005).

span.label: 900 ms — length of the memory period over which modulation persisted in the static-texture control experiment
span.quote: Also in this experiment, contextual modulation continued during the whole period (900 ms) that the animal had to remember the figure location (Fig. 2E).

span.label: P , 1025 — significance of the correct-versus-incorrect difference in modulation in the final 250 ms before cue time (initial 250 ms did not differ, P . 0.1)
span.quote: Analysis of individual recording sites (Fig. 3, E and F) showed that the strength of the figure-ground signal during the first 250 ms after stimulus onset was similar for the correct and incorrect trails (P . 0.1 for both delay periods), but that most electrodes showed stronger modulation at the final 250 ms before cue time for correct trials compared with incorrect trials (P , 1025 for both delay periods).

span.label: two monkeys — number of animals from which V1 multiunit activity was recorded
span.quote: During the delayed-response task, multiunit activity of V1 neurons was recorded in two monkeys (2).
